articles.title: Two more people rescued in Nepal 10 days after devastating floods
articles.summary: Rescuers pulled a Chinese man from a hydropower tunnel and found a 60-year-old woman alive in a four-story building following flash floods on the border with China. Follow for live updates.
articles.body:
• Dramatic rescue: Two more people have been rescued in Nepal, 10 days after devastating flash floods on the border with China. A Chinese man was pulled alive from a tunnel at a hydropower plant and a 60-year-old woman was rescued from the upper floor of a four-story building.

• Second in as many days: Two men were dramatically pulled alive from another hydropower tunnel in Nepal yesterday. Rescuers had to use satellite pictures to find the tunnel below the mud. Hundreds of tunnel workers remain missing following the disaster.

• Death toll climbs: The number of people killed in last week’s catastrophic flash floods has now risen to 1,375, according to a CNN tally of figures published by Nepali and Chinese authorities.

Rescue efforts have focused on the various hydropower projects dotted along the Trishuli River where hundreds of workers are trapped after last week’s flash floods encased the facilities in mud.

Around 900 workers were still recorded as missing, the Nepali Army said on Thursday, two-thirds of whom were at the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project.

That is the plant from where Lu Haitao was rescued today.

Each hydropower project presents its own challenges to rescuers who are trying to find the safest way in. Some have internal tunnels stretching several kilometers, meaning any surviving workers could be a long way from the portal.

Rooms and resources inside the tunnels could theoretically help any trapped workers to survive – potentially for weeks, though air supply could be another problem.

Teams are using all sorts of technology to help locate any survivors. They’ve used satellite data, drawings of the power station and topographic information to find a way into the tunnels, according to Arnold Dix, a geologist advising the operations, as well as thermal cameras on drones to search for survivors.

Nine days after flash flooding washed away valleys and buried entire villages, rescue workers in Nepal had started to shift their operations from finding survivors to recovering bodies.

But then on Friday morning, at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant, they heard an unmistakeable sound: “Okay.”

In a dramatic breakthrough for what has been a desperate, round-the-clock rescue effort in treacherous conditions, two men were pulled from an underground chamber of the hydropower plant, where Nepali rescue crews had been boring in search of 42 missing workers.

Rescuers had earlier reported hearing voices after days of a complex search and clearing mission, according to Bipin Regmi, police chief in the flood-hit district of Nuwakot.

Through a patchwork of grey debris, the two men emerged.

Carried out on a rescuer’s back, Sanjay Sah raised his hand in a wave before resting his head on the Nepal Army rescuer’s helmet. His first question was: “What day is it?”

The second man, Kabir Maharjan, was placed on a stretcher with an oxygen mask over his face.

That moment was the culmination of nine days of work that started with almost nothing to go on. After the August 26 disaster, the Trishuli 3A power station was unrecognizable and initially Nepali rescuers had no idea where to start digging.

To find a way in, the team had to work off satellite data, as-built drawings of the power station and topographic information, according to Arnold Dix, a geologist advising Nepali rescuers on the ground.

That’s how they narrowed down the location of the tunnel least likely to have collapsed – an area Dix calls the “Goldilocks zone.”

Rescue efforts in the hydropower tunnels where hundreds of workers are feared missing are underway and will continue for a “few days,” according to Suresh Raut, a deputy manager at the Nepal Electricity Authority.

Joint teams from Nepal’s police, army and other officials are scouring the tunnels in different power stations along the Trishuli River for survivors with the help of emergency lights, Raut said.

With today’s rescue, three workers in total have been found alive in the past 48 hours days on from the catastrophic floods.

The death toll from last week’s catastrophic flash floods in Nepal and China has risen to 1,375, according to authorities on both sides of the border, with more than 5,000 people still missing.

Rescuers today found two survivors, 10 days after the flooding wrought havoc on the border between the two countries.

Rescuers in Nepal have pulled a Chinese national alive from a hydropower tunnel. The Nepali army has said he is named Lu Haitao and that his health is being assessed.

A woman, 60, has also been rescued from a building in the Nepali district of Nuwakot, according to the Nepal armed police force.

At least 1,344 people have died in Nepal and 4,898 people are still missing because of the flooding, Nepali police said in an update this morning.

Meanwhile in China, at least 31 people have been killed and another 531 are unaccounted for in the autonomous region of Tibet, according to state news agency Xinhua.

58 people were rescued in Nepal yesterday, the army said, with the help of seven army aircrafts and six civilian aircrafts.

Dozens of Nepali villagers who were stranded by the floods lined up for days to return home via a makeshift zip line yesterday.

CNN’s Bhadra Sharma, Kathleen Magramo, Kosh Raj Koirala, Charlotte Reck, Sarah Hutter and Zahid Mahmood contributed to this reporting.

A team of South Korean rescue workers helped the Nepali Army rescue Chinese national Lu Haitao from inside a hydropower tunnel earlier today, Nepal’s Prime Minister’s Office just said.

Rescuers have been working for days to find any survivors from the catastrophic flash floods which tore through the country last week, leaving at least 1,000 dead and thousands more missing.

It has now been 10 days since catastrophic flooding hit the Nepal-China border, killing at least 1,375 people, according to authorities in both countries.

Rescuers are still working to find survivors, with more than 5,000 people still missing, as locals grapple with the destruction left in the wake of the floods.

Here’s a look at the latest from the ground:

A woman has been rescued from a building in the Nepali district of Nuwakot ten days after devastating floods swept through the area, according to the Nepal armed police force.

The 60-year old woman had been trapped on the upper floor of a four-storey building.

In their statement, the Nepali Army named the Chinese national they rescued as Lu Haitao and said his health is being assessed.

“A joint rescue team comprising the Nepali Army and foreign rescuers has rescued a Chinese national, Lu Haitao, alive from inside a tunnel at the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project,” the army said following the rescue on Saturday afternoon local time.

“Lu Haitao was rescued from a point approximately 225 meters inside the tunnel. His health is currently being assessed, while search and rescue operations are continuing.”

Rescuers in Nepal have pulled a Chinese national alive from a hydropower tunnel 10 days after floods caused devastation on the border, according to the Nepali army.

We’ll bring you more on this developing story as we get it.

articles.title: A Texas teenager started building birdhouses after losing his pet cockatiel; 5 years later, he has made 750 shelters and inspired a conservation movement across 20 states
articles.summary: US News: Aamir Tinwala, a middle-schooler living through pandemic isolation begged his parents for a pet and they agreed to get him a bird, a bright yellow-fac.
articles.body: Aamir Tinwala, a middle-schooler living through pandemic isolation begged his parents for a pet and they agreed to get him a bird, a bright yellow-faced and orange-cheeked cockatiel, whom he named Koco. This bond, inspired the Texas teen to launch a bird conservation movement that is now spread across continents and generations according to a Washington Post report.Aamir's connection and attachment to Koco was instant and she soon became a household fixture. He learned about the decline in wild bird populations and decided to build birdhouses in his backyard to compensate for widespread habitat loss. His Backyard Bird Project helps establish safe habitats for birds in urban and suburban areas while connecting people to local biodiversity issues.The teenager coordinated with neighbours, schools, and community groups to help build nesting boxes. He created a website to encourage people to register for boxes, which he then built and shipped. He also provided instructions for people to build their own boxes and help the movement grow.Strategically placed nest boxes provide shelter and breeding areas for birds, supporting thriving species populations. His project has also helped young people become interested in birding and habitat stewardship. "It had actual tangible benefits," he told the Post. "Other than just me hacking away every day in my garage."To date, he has personally built over 750 bird shelters in the past five years and helped countless others build their own. In a separate effort, he launched a successful petition to have his hometown name a city bird, the American kestrel.Meanwhile, many other bird conservation efforts are underway to rescue at-risk birds, rehabilitate injured birds, and rediscover rare birds once thought to be extinct. "It's a small thing to do," he said, of his nesting box building. "But it is also considerable. If everyone did it, an actual impact would be made."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Rescuers in Nepal pull out two more people alive 10 days after devastating floods
articles.summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal pulled a man and a woman alive 10 days after devastating floods hit the country, officials said Saturday.
articles.body: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal pulled a man and a woman alive 10 days after devastating floods hit the country, officials said Saturday. The man, a Chinese national, was rescued from a hydropower tunnel, according to a social media post by the country’s prime minister’s office, bringing the total to three workers pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower project. Two Nepalese workers were rescued from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant on Friday. Nepal’s army said a joint rescue team of Nepalese military personnel and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-meter tunnel (about 738 feet) and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Images showed him being evacuated by helicopter, with an army medic checking on him during the flight. A photo released by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed two rescuers carrying the man out of the tunnel. About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects across Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. In flood-hit Nuwakot town, a woman was rescued alive from a house, Nepal’s army spokesperson said Saturday. Officials said she was being airlifted to Kathmandu. Images showed rescuers pulling the woman from the house, wrapped in a gray blanket. At least 1,300 people were killed in the Aug. 26 floods, which were likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

articles.title: Oil and politics: What Trump’s ‘historic’ deal means for Venezuela
articles.summary: Venezuelans are hoping for free and fair elections, but the US may prioritise oil production.
articles.body:
Since the last century, Venezuelan politics has been closely linked to the management of the country’s oil industry.

The debate for policymakers has centred on whether to liberalise or nationalise the sector, with the latter being the preferred option for the past 27 years.

Over time, a kind of “resource nationalism” has been instilled in the national psyche by the current governing party to consolidate its power and advance the interests of a regime that has used oil revenues to expand its political influence across the region, particularly in the Caribbean.

This all came to an abrupt end on January 3, 2026, when United States special forces abducted President Nicolas Maduro in a lightning military operation in Caracas and whisked him back to the US to stand trial on guns-and-drugs charges.

Since then, Maduro’s deputy and now interim President Delcy Rodriguez has aimed for privatisation of the oil industry in favour of US government interests.

Milestones reached during the past eight months include reforming the General Hydrocarbons Law, liberalising energy power plants and granting permissions, with prior US authorisation, to US and foreign oil companies – excluding any from China, Russia, Iran or North Korea – to participate in tapping Venezuela’s vast oil wealth in oil fields across the country.

The most significant development happened last week, when the two countries announced they had reached a deal granting US companies access to 65 billion barrels of crude oil reserves over the next 100 years.

Described by President Trump as the “biggest oil deal in world history”, this agreement not only marks a turning point in the governing party’s resource nationalism policy but also represents the culmination of the US government’s efforts to reinforce its dominance strategy and seize control of Venezuela’s oil and gas resources.

Furthermore, this deal is set to play a pivotal role in the Venezuelan political transition.

The US has developed a three-phase plan to promote stabilisation, recovery, and political reform since it removed Maduro from power. Now, all the parties involved must establish a roadmap to implement the deal and, at the same time, ensure that presidential elections are held in the country.

The signing of this oil deal is the starting gun for this complex process.

A win for the US – not so much for Venezuela

The precise terms of this oil deal have been the subject of discussion in specialised media outlets across the Western Hemisphere and beyond this week. Due to conflicting and sometimes contradictory accounts by US and Venezuelan authorities, the final conditions of the oil deal remain uncertain.

The Trump Administration has provided the most detailed information, confirming the transfer of 65 billion barrels of oil – 20 percent of Venezuela’s proven 303 billion barrels of oil – to US control for 100 years.

These reserves are distributed across 17 major oil fields, some of which had previously been granted to Chinese and Russian companies in concession. The fields will be operated by a private company called North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), in association with the US Department of Defense’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC). This entity will acquire a 35 percent stake in NABEP free of charge. Trump has referred to the latter to argue that this association will not charge American taxpayers or use their money.

Additionally, information from the US government suggests that the US has also secured the right to buy 20 percent of the current and future crude oil production from NABEP-controlled fields at production cost. That means production will not be subject to Venezuelan taxation, reducing the amount of revenue Venezuela will receive.

The OSC has the right of first refusal to buy the remaining 80 percent of production, or veto power if this is deemed necessary for reasons of national security. These clauses prioritise ensuring the US has access to Venezuelan oil reserves and meeting the requirements of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR). These measures are undoubtedly intended to help the US achieve its national energy security goals.

The White House has also confirmed that NABEP is controlled by American citizens, which is a prerogative reserved by the US government to prevent foreign companies from managing it. In practice, this means that the US will control the operations, with NABEP merely acting as a vehicle for this control.

Another point relates to the royalties and taxes that NABEP must pay to the Venezuelan authorities. Top officials from both countries say the exploitation of the 17 oil fields will generate approximately $200bn dollars in tax payments following an expected $100bn investment. It is expected that this money will be managed by the current interim authorities to address the challenges of reconstruction after a long period of economic crisis.

However, there is uncertainty about the methodology used to determine this amount because the discretionary clauses granted to the US government make it impossible to calculate the exact amount of tax that will be paid.

Furthermore, the Venezuelan government has announced that the concession granted to NABEP will only be valid for 25 years – a figure far lower than the 100 years claimed by the US government. Notably, this type of contract has not featured in Venezuelan hydrocarbon legislation for half a century.

Although the bilateral agreement could be a good way to attract investment to the Venezuelan oil sector, there remain multiple internal and external political, legal and economic obstacles to its successful implementation.

First, President Trump has so far failed to encourage major US oil companies, except Chevron, to enter the Venezuelan oil industry. This is because Venezuela lacks trustworthy and legitimate institutions, implying the absence of a stable legal framework for long-term production planning.

Setting aside the major oil companies such as Exxon Mobil, Chevron and ConocoPhillips, the only companies that appear as viable potential partners in the 17 oil fields seem to be small independent operators. This could lead to operational setbacks because the majors are the only ones with enough financial and technological clout to carry out long-term, large-scale investments in such ambitious projects.

The oil majors’ lack of confidence is also down to the absence of a legitimate government and the governing party’s continued dominance over the country’s main powers.

One of the biggest red flags surrounding the oil deal is the possibility that a government formed through free elections could in the future denounce or refuse to recognise its legitimacy, on the basis that these legal agreements are unconstitutional. Furthermore, the current governing party in Venezuela could potentially reject the terms of this deal if they feel they have sufficient strength to challenge US dominance again.

In addition to these concerns about the rule of law, it seems there is another relevant issue: The involvement of Alejandro Betancourt as president of NABEP’s operations.

Despite the Department of State’s attempts to clean up his past, Betancourt has an uncertain record due to multiple corruption cases brought against him in the past, including bribery, cost overruns and influence peddling in electricity projects overseen by the state-owned company PDVSA.

It is also important to note that a real, feasible increase in Venezuelan oil production will probably take several years, even in the best-case scenario. This contradicts the optimistic rhetoric used by senior Trump administration officials, who argue that this deal would increase local production almost immediately. Advancing at such a pace would require substantial investment, much of which is not currently guaranteed.

Approval of the oil deal is part of a broader “hemispheric” strategy adopted by the US government, which wants to regain lost influence in the region. This was outlined in the Trump administration’s 2025 National Security Strategy and subsequent foreign policy documents, which designate the Western Hemisphere as a strategic zone of influence for the US. In this context, the US government views Venezuela as a strategic geopolitical pivot due to its energy resources – particularly its substantial proven oil reserves – and its proximity to its territory.

Based on this, the US government considers controlling the Venezuelan oil reserves to be a matter of national security that is closely linked to maintaining its SPR. This stance is particularly pertinent given that Washington is preventing countries it considers to be its enemies, such as China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, from participating in the Venezuelan oil industry.

It is also worth noting that the US government is not hesitating to use its existing national tools to secure its hegemony across the Americas. Indeed, the US is taking economic measures, as well as military action and exerting political influence, to discourage other countries from doing business with its declared enemies, including China, and even more so from allowing them to participate in critical infrastructure projects across the region.

Since its removal of Maduro from power in January, the US government has begun a three-phase plan to promote stabilisation, economic recovery and political reform in Venezuela. The ultimate objective is to hold free and democratic elections, which would be the first step towards legitimising the country’s authorities and reintegrating it into the international arena.

Before this week’s oil deal was announced, various opposition leaders had been devising strategies to participate in the eventual presidential elections. These actors believed that the electoral process was the first step in recovering sovereignty and establishing a long-term partnership with the US based on oil business.

However, the plan of Trump’s administration has run in a different direction and at its own pace. For Washington, securing access to and control of the Venezuelan oil reservoirs was the top priority before promoting any democratic transition in the country.

Although top US officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have recently stated that the oil deal is limited to its own three-phase plan, the reality is that the US has made it clear that it will not allow any future government to change its terms and conditions.

Given the current situation, almost everyone involved in Venezuelan politics supports an oil deal that prioritises the participation of the US. However, opposition leaders such as Maria Corina Machado , currently the country’s most popular politician, are concerned about Delcy Rodriguez, an interim leader who lacks legitimacy, signing this deal.

Although Machado has not guaranteed that a future democratic government would refuse to recognise the deal’s terms, her position could spur the idea that Trump is motivated to keep Delcy Rodriguez in power rather than promote free elections to ensure the deal’s correct implementation.

These concerns have arisen in recent days after the US president publicly stated that Venezuela is not prepared for elections in the short term.

Ultimately, the effectiveness of the oil deal and its impact on the political transition in Venezuela will depend on the alignment of various internal and external political, legal, and economic factors.

For now, the US government holds the final say in determining the country’s future, to the detriment of its population, which has ultimately lost its right to self-determination.

articles.title: American Airlines passenger duct-taped to seat after alleged racist, homophobic midair outburst
articles.summary: Video and photos show passengers restraining a man with duct tape and zip ties on an American Airlines flight after a violent and racist midair outburst.
articles.body: A passenger on an American Airlines flight was restrained to his seat with duct tape and zip ties after a midair outburst, forcing the plane to be diverted. The flight from Dallas-Fort Worth to Newark, New Jersey, had to make an unexpected stop in Baltimore late Thursday night due to the unidentified disruptive passenger who witnesses said was putting others at risk. The man was allegedly screaming racial and homophobic slurs during the outburst, according to TMZ. Video footage of the incident shows crew and passengers strapping the man to his seat as he appeared to put up a fight. Photos show the man secured to his seat with duct tape and zip ties, with even his head held to the seat. FLIGHT PASSENGER YELLS, 'I WANT OFF,' CALLS CREW 'IDIOTS' AND YANKS OPEN EMERGENCY EXIT DOOR Witnesses said the chaos erupted about two hours into the flight, when the man began yelling at a male passenger next to him. According to TMZ, the man was screaming about Jesus and going to hell, prompting a flight attendant to walk over and attempt to calm the situation. The man called the flight attendant, who is Black, a racial slur and also shouted anti-gay remarks, according to the outlet. The man also reportedly became violent as he hit the passenger next to him. A female passenger jumped in to help, but the man pushed her, leading to three other male passengers stepping in, the outlet reported. UNITED FLIGHT FROM CHICAGO MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER PASSENGER'S 'MULTIPLE ATTEMPTS' TO BREACH COCKPIT "Just like a light switch, all of a sudden, it went from quiet to yelling and chaos," one of the men, retired law enforcement officer Juan Mejia, told CBS Texas. "I turned around to look, and the poor gentleman that was sitting next to him in the aisle seat, the individual had his hands around his neck and was, like, assaulting him." Flight attendants handed duct tape and zip ties to the three male passengers, who restrained the unruly man to his seat and held him down as he attempted to break free. American Airlines and the Federal Aviation Administration confirmed the plane was diverted to Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport, where law enforcement took the man into custody. "On Sept. 3, ​American Airlines ​flight 618 diverted ​to ​Baltimore (BWI) ​due to a disruptive customer," the airline said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Upon arrival, law enforcement met ​the ​aircraft ​and ​assisted ​with ​deplaning the ​customer before the ​flight ​continued to its ​destination." "The safety ​and ​security ​of our customers ​and team members ​is our top ​priority and ​we ​do not ​tolerate violence. We thank our ​team members for ​their ​professionalism ​and ​our customers ​for ​their ​understanding," the statement added. The FBI said that the Maryland Transportation Police arrested and booked the man on state charges. articles.title: How Cubans are navigating the US oil blockade with rechargeable fans and solar-powered Chinese tricycles
articles.summary: The US oil blockade is forcing Cubans to think outside the box for tasks that usually require electricity. Farmers pasteurize milk over charcoal fires, commuters ride solar-powered Chinese tricycles, tour guides grind coffee by hand for the vanishingly few visitors that remain.
articles.body: How to conserve cellphone battery when recharging options are scarce; how to preserve food when the fridge isn’t working; how to cope with the heat when air-conditioners aren’t an option; how to generate power when the whole country has almost none left. These are the sort of tutorials that have made the Instagram feed of influencer Dayán Marrero indispensable to many Cubans as they try to adapt to the rolling electricity blackouts and fuel shortages that are increasingly part of everyday life on this Caribbean island. As the US-imposed oil blockade that is worsening the situation bites ever deeper, Marrero and his compatriots are having to get creative. Farmers pasteurize milk over charcoal fires; commuters ride solar-powered Chinese tricycles; tour guides grind coffee by hand for the vanishingly few visitors that remain. Like his fellow countrymen, Marrero — a third-year computer science student at the Agrarian University of Havana — has become adept at adapting. Previously, the idea that he might become a content creator had “never even crossed my mind,” yet here he is, in the living room of his home in Caraballo, a former sugar town, promoting the latest must-have items, such as a rechargeable fan that also provides light while he records his videos. And he is successful; one of his most popular posts, a tutorial on how to build an antenna to pick up the mobile network’s elusive internet signal, is approaching 800,000 views. Still, if he is to reach his next goal as an influencer — establishing a presence on TikTok — he will have to get even more creative, as use of the app is restricted by US sanctions. Tourism without tourists Cubans have known for decades what it is like to live without abundance and — while it is true that things have worsened markedly since the US blockade and the subsequent loss of energy imports from both Venezuela and Mexico — people like Marrero are showing there is no scarcity of creativity or resilience on this island. At 57 years old, Osiris Hernández has spent more than half his life as a tour guide in Viñales, Cuba’s ecotourism mecca. He works at one of Viñales’ main tourist attractions, the Indian Cave, where he operates a boat that carries visitors through waters deep underground and ends its journey with a spectacular view as it emerges from darkness into light. The streets in Viñales are clean, signs advertising rooms for visitors are everywhere and there is even a market where artisans sell their wares. There’s just one problem: There are almost no tourists. Tourism on the island fell 62% from January to July compared with the same period last year, according to official figures. When Hernández hears a single Chinese tourist has arrived, a smile crosses his face. He is eager to please the few who, despite it all, still come to visit. He has set up rooms in his own home to accommodate them and cooks their food over charcoal, grinds coffee by hand and passes around the same type of rechargeable, light-providing fan that Marrero advertises on his Instagram. He tells CNN his goal is to provide quality service, whatever is happening with the electricity. Even when the power is down, he says, he has an inverter that converts energy from solar panels for use in household appliances. It allows him to keep at least one freezer running. Pasteurizing with charcoal On the outskirts of Viñales is El Olivo agroecological farm, where Osnel Corrales and his family have installed solar panels and batteries to help them produce dairy. Although they have an industrial generator, they do not have fuel, or at least not enough. On the day CNN visited, they were producing yogurt — pasteurizing the milk first by heating it over charcoal, then cooling it in vats using electricity generated by solar panels. The farm has a restaurant specializing in Mediterranean food, but there are no customers. Yet they continue operating — the cows have to be milked no matter what — and produce cheese in addition to their yogurt, which they distribute through a branded store in Viñales and to customers in Havana. Still, the lack of tourists means demand for their award-winning produce has dropped severely and given the shortage of fuel it’s not easy for the few tourists still arriving in Cuba to visit the farm. A glimmer of light on the roads The lack of fuel, however, does have one silver lining: Traffic congestion in Havana feels like a thing of the past. With buses in short supply, a growing fleet of privately operated solar-powered electric tricycles provide public transportation for the city’s nearly 1.8 million residents. Augusto operates one of the latest-generation models. Not only does it have a small fuel-powered engine but, more importantly, it has three rechargeable batteries. He can connect these to the power grid — when there is electricity — or charge them via the solar panel that serves as the vehicle’s roof. Augusto, who has spent years driving taxis, rents the tricycle for about 9,000 Cuban pesos ($15) per day, whether or not he has passengers. It can carry up to six passengers at a time, in a system in which operators have strategically divided the city into routes that take into account the distance they can travel based on battery range and the available charge level. With or without fuel, Augusto manages to help his fellow Cubans get around every day by relying on a dynamic that is long familiar on the island. Augusto, Marrero, Hernández and countless others have little choice but to figure things out which, in Cuban parlance, means overcoming whatever obstacle is placed in their way.

articles.title: If ‘fall is really the new summer,’ are there any autumn travel deals left?
articles.summary: The secret’s out about traveling in the fall and prices are rising. The value hasn’t completely dried up, but it’s not automatic, experts say.
articles.body: Heather Wright has long been a fan of off-season travel, when the weather cools, crowds thin and prices drop significantly. At least, that used to be the pattern heading into fall. Wright, a tax accountant from Seattle, has been looking to take a trip with friends to Europe in November, possibly to Malta or Madeira. She plans to fly into whichever major European airport she can comfortably reach from the US for a good deal and take shorter flights onward from there. But she’s not finding the savings she expected. “This fall is kind of weird. It just feels like the prices are a lot higher later into the season than they have been in the past,” said Wright, who has focused mostly on tracking airfare. She’s not wrong. Surging jet fuel prices caused by the war with Iran sent fares way up this year. And the broader travel savings long associated with the shift from summer to fall have been shrinking for several years as demand for autumn travel grows. Finding fall value is still possible, some experts say. But travelers will need to be more flexible and strategic. It’s clear that the “secret season” is no longer a secret, especially among luxury travelers. “Our perspective is that fall is really the new summer,” said Misty Belles, vice president of global public relations for Virtuoso, a network that specializes in luxury and experiential travel. Fading fall savings Virtuoso is seeing a 59% increase in fall 2026 bookings over last year, with the amount of money generated off fall bookings up 69%. Virtuoso’s bookings to Europe this fall have climbed 49%, even as rates rose more than 7%, “showing that travelers are choosing the season for what it offers rather than what it saves,” Belles noted in a recent presentation. (Virtuoso’s figures are based almost entirely on high-end hotel insights). Higher prices aren’t limited to international luxury travel. In the US, autumn savings on domestic airfare have pretty much dried up. “It seems like this year, there is not going to be a shoulder season for domestic travelers,” said Hayley Berg, lead travel economist for travel technology platform Hopper Technology Solutions (HTS). HTS shows average domestic fall airfare is up 39% compared to last year ­— putting ticket prices in line with peak summer months for the first time in years. Four years ago, the cost of US domestic airfare in the fall was about 20% less than peak summer. This year, it’s 1% higher, according to HTS. The company points to this year’s fuel shock, increased demand driven by flexible remote work arrangements and less competition from low-cost carriers as factors in the disappearance of discounts. Expedia has found that prices this fall in its top 10 US destinations, including New York, Miami and New Orleans, are higher than this summer, with lodging costs up an average of 20% and flight prices 2% higher. But the travel company also pointed to US beach and mountain destinations where significant fall savings are possible, including Fort Walton Beach, Florida, and Aspen, Colorado. US travelers aren’t the only ones facing high autumn prices. Expedia also found that fall hotel stays in destinations across the United Kingdom are, on average, slightly higher than summer, with some spots up as much as 20% to 30%. But some destinations in Portugal’s Algarve region and the Greek islands offer significant savings, the company pointed out. “Fall travel savings aren’t gone, but they’re not automatic,” said Melanie Fish, head of public relations for Expedia Group. Searching for fall value As dynamic pricing has spread more widely into the lodging sector, largely gone are the days when hoteliers automatically dropped prices as calendars flipped to September. For fall savings “it’s just as much about flexibility for where you go as scheduling that trip right after Labor Day,” Fish said. Travelers are searching on Expedia Group sites such as Expedia.com and Hotels.com using budget filters, Fish said, and “they’re using their rewards, they’re bundling perks and other ways to stretch the value of a trip” beyond just picking a date after the holiday weekend. Berg says looking at different airports within the same state or region can yield savings. Being flexible on your destination within the framework of a certain type of getaway — a beach vacation, for example — helps. And choosing dates that don’t make for the very popular Thursday-to-Sunday trip can be a cost-saver. “Sunday is typically the cheapest day of the week to stay,” Fish said. “So if you can plan your shoulder-season trip over a Sunday, then you have a double chance of getting some savings there.” Airfares will drop for most international regions going into fall, compared to summer 2026 fares — but by less than in recent years. In 2023, Europe fares dropped by 33% from summer to fall; this year HTS says that summer-to-fall drop will be 22%. “So the savings percentage versus summer is still there. It’s just that prices are so much higher across the board that you’re still going to be paying more this year,” Berg said. Airfares to Europe this fall are up 33% compared to last fall, according to HTS. ‘September has really replaced August’ It’s no surprise that the increasingly relentless heat of summer is a key driver of the shift toward fall travel. Crowds are another huge factor. And travelers have more flexibility. Even families tied to school calendars are increasingly taking advantage of short school breaks spread throughout the year, according to Jo-Anne Redwood, a travel adviser in southern California with Luna World Travel, which is a Virtuoso member. Redwood was reminded this summer of why she never suggests August to her clients. She spent a few sweltering weeks in Europe in July and August, in part to participate in what’s known as a “familiarization trip” to learn more about offerings from a luxury cruise line. Peak summer was the only time it was available. “It was miserable,” she said. On a tour she took in Budapest, one woman fainted. Redwood said the temperature was close to 100 degrees Fahrenheit with 80% humidity. Redwood’s affluent clients are prioritizing the comfort that fall offers, both through lower temperatures and fewer crowds. “September has really replaced August and October is replacing September … I’m very, very busy right now with late September, October and even November cruising,” Redwood said. And prices are reflecting the high demand for fall trips. She was researching river cruises for late October and early November recently and she said prices are 15% to 20% higher — about $1,000 more — for those dates than they are for early September this year. And hotel rooms at smaller luxury properties with fewer rooms are becoming increasingly scarce. “I just tried to book the Rosewood in Tuscany for October, and the only room that’s left is $17,000 a night,” she said. While that highest-end price is eye-popping, increases are evident across the spectrum. “So on the higher end, yes, I am finding availability is a challenge in October. On the lower end, I think there’s still a lot of availability, but you’re just paying more for it,” Redwood said. The surge in interest among some travelers doesn’t necessarily mean that overall travel volume has been spiking this year. According to data tracked by analytics firm Cirium, a significant sample of airline booking data from online travel agencies and the global distribution system (GDS) for airlines suggests that bookings from the US to Europe for this July declined by about 6% from July 2025. And data for tickets booked over the summer for travel this fall suggests a similar nearly 6% autumn dip for travel from the US to Europe, compared to the same period last year. But Belles noted generally that bookings look higher in the luxury market, where traveler appetites closely mirror the performance of the stock market, which has been booming this year. She also pointed to the continued trend of prioritizing experiences over goods. And the experiences many Virtuoso travelers are seeking involve having more of a destination to themselves. That could be why interest in traveling in November is surging, too. Belles said it used to be a month that travelers mostly skipped over because of US Thanksgiving, “so now to see that we’re up like 70 and 71% for bookings and sales for November is really pretty staggering to me,” she said. A standoff for savings? Wright, the Seattle accountant, clearly has plenty of company as she eyes a late-fall break in Europe. Wright is hoping to fly premium economy or business class, but only if she can find a good deal. She’s planning to use credit card miles for at least part of her fare. Wright has noticed that one-way cash prices, which she has typically found to be closer to the price of a roundtrip fare, are now closer to half the roundtrip price. She’s thinking about mixing and matching one-way tickets, possibly in different cabin classes, paid for through a combination of cash and loyalty miles, to make her trip happen. But Wright is also noticing plenty of empty seats on the flights she’s been considering and is confounded by the high prices. “I’m just wondering if there’s a standoff between travelers and the airlines, where everyone is waiting to see who will blink first,” she said in an email to CNN Travel. “I suspect the airlines, knowing that fall travel is now much more popular than in the past, and that certain pockets of the population are still doing really well, are trying to sell as many expensive seats as early as they can, while waiting to see what happens with fuel costs,” Wright said. For now, she said she’s “in a holding pattern,” monitoring tickets to see what kind of fall value she can find. “I just don’t want to break the bank for a November trip. That just seems crazy to me.”

articles.title: Russia's shadow war is putting Europe on edge as Germany confronts a growing threat
articles.summary: Germany accused Russia of a drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport and now pushes Baltic Sea allies to form a rapid-response hybrid warfare task force.
articles.body: Germany is pushing European partners to create a rapid-response task force in the Baltic Sea region as Berlin confronts what it says is an escalating campaign of Russian hybrid warfare, including an attempted explosives-laden drone attack on one of the country's most important cargo airports. The initiative, proposed by German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt following an Aug. 28 meeting in Flensburg, is intended to allow Baltic Sea countries to rapidly exchange information and coordinate responses to hybrid threats ranging from drones and sabotage to cyberattacks, disinformation and attacks on critical infrastructure. "We want to turn this shared threat environment into a shared security environment," Dobrindt said, warning that hybrid threats were becoming more frequent and sophisticated. The proposal has taken on new urgency after Germany formally accused Russia this week of responsibility for an attempted Aug. 4 attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport involving a drone carrying explosives. EXPLOSIVE DRONE FORCES SHUTDOWN AT MAJOR GERMAN AIRPORT SERVING NATO, UKRAINE FLIGHTS German officials said police findings, intelligence information and the methods used in the attack led Berlin to conclude Russia was responsible. The government said aspects of the drone, explosives and detonation technology were consistent with methods seen in previous Russian hybrid operations and in Moscow's war against Ukraine. Germany has not publicly released much of the underlying evidence, saying details including information about suspected perpetrators, travel routes, surveillance footage and DNA evidence are being withheld to protect the investigation. Latvia characterized the Leipzig attack in even stronger terms. "The attack in Leipzig confirms once again that Russia poses a direct threat to the security of all of Europe. This was not merely a hybrid attack, but state-sponsored terrorism on German soil," Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said in a statement published by Latvia's Foreign Ministry. Braže also called for continued efforts to strengthen Ukraine's defense capabilities and for additional sanctions aimed at limiting Russia's ability to produce missiles, drones and other weapons. US INTEL WARNS RUSSIA COULD LAUNCH LIMITED ATTACK ON NATO ALLY IN EFFORT TO FRAGMENT ORGANIZATION: REPORT Retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Richard Newton told Fox News Digital that the episode reflects what he described as a widening pattern of hostile activity. "We are clearly seeing an escalation in the scope and intensity of Russian gray-zone hostile actions across Europe," Newton said. "Russia has long used a variety of non-military, covert, and hybrid tactics – cyberattacks, information operations, sabotage, other covert means – to create disruption while staying just below the threshold of open conflict with NATO." Newton called Germany's attribution of the Leipzig plot "particularly serious," saying it "demonstrates how dangerous these operations are becoming." Germany responded by announcing the closure of Russia's consulate general in Bonn and ending the arrangement governing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin. Berlin also said it would tighten entry controls for Russian nationals and increase pressure on Russia's so-called shadow fleet. Russia has denied responsibility for the Leipzig incident, calling Germany's accusations "entirely fabricated" and accusing Berlin of escalating tensions, according to Reuters. The heightened concern comes as German police separately investigate a cluster of suspected sabotage incidents targeting the country's electricity infrastructure this week. REPORT WARNS RUSSIA USING SHADOW FLEET TO PROBE NATO DRONE DEFENSES Authorities were investigating a suspicious device found near a substation in Dormagen, North Rhine-Westphalia, on Friday, following incidents in Bergheim and Brandenburg. In Bergheim, deliberate interference temporarily forced lignite-fired generating units representing about 4,200 megawatts of capacity offline, though no broader blackout occurred. German authorities have not publicly connected those power-grid incidents to Russia, a distinction Newton said was important. "We need to be careful when attributing these hostile acts and ensure we have indisputable intelligence information that clearly leads to the source of these belligerent actions," Newton said. "The incidents involving Germany’s power infrastructure are still under investigation and have not been publicly attributed to Russia, or any other source for that matter," he added. The German government nevertheless said Friday that the country faces a persistent hybrid threat. "Germany is not at war, but it is a daily target of hybrid warfare," the government said, citing attacks on communications systems, disinformation and arson targeting the defense industry. EUROPE BANKROLLS PUTIN'S WAR MACHINE EVEN AS NATO RACES TO BOLSTER DEFENSES Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told Fox News Digital that Moscow has increasingly sought to pressure Western countries while avoiding conventional conflict. "We do know that Russia is trying to fight the Western world below the line of kinetic conflict and their methods are getting ever bolder, whether through cyber operations, sabotage, drones and other forms of pressure across Europe," Breedlove said. "We’re even becoming aware of things they are doing inside the United States." Breedlove said Russian President Vladimir Putin has long sought to exploit divisions within NATO, "especially between the United States and Europe." "The Western world has got to step up to counter the Russian threat," he said. The Baltic initiative comes amid broader efforts by NATO and regional governments to protect an area increasingly associated with threats to undersea cables, pipelines, shipping and other critical infrastructure. NATO already operates Baltic Sentry, an enhanced vigilance activity launched in 2025 to strengthen protection of critical undersea infrastructure in the Baltic Sea. In February, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Sweden agreed to accelerate the acquisition and integration of new technologies for Baltic naval operations. NATO said that initiative built on testing involving roughly 70 aerial and maritime drones in 2025. Breedlove said Germany's proposed task force could help bridge intelligence, law-enforcement and military responses among regional partners. "Germany’s Baltic initiative makes sense," he said. "The value is also for partner countries to share information faster, connect the intelligence, law-enforcement and military pieces, and make decisions before Russia can take advantage of confusion or delay." Newton similarly said the task force could complement NATO's existing military activity by improving governments' ability to rapidly share intelligence and coordinate security responses. Breedlove warned that Moscow would continue searching for opportunities to exploit uncertainty. "Without question, the Russians will keep looking for places where they can create uncertainty and hesitation," he said. "We need to get better at recognizing their actions with speed – and responding forcefully with the strength of our allies." articles.title: Charles Manson's 'Helter Skelter' motive a myth? New tapes reveal what may have sparked Sharon Tate murders
articles.summary: Joe Berlinger's Netflix docuseries argues the Charles Manson murders were not about starting a race war but covering up a drug deal gone bad.
articles.body: For decades, the prevailing story of the Manson murders held that Charles Manson masterminded a murderous plot to ignite a race war inspired by the Beatles. But Joe Berlinger argues the infamous story never added up. The true crime filmmaker directed a three-part Netflix docuseries titled "Conversations with a Killer: The Charles Manson Tapes." It features previously unreleased prison audio from the cult leader and some of his "Manson Family" members. In 1969, the career criminal who surrounded himself with runaways and other lost souls directed his followers to commit a series of murders in and around Los Angeles. Prosecutors argued the killings were part of Manson's "Helter Skelter" plan to ignite a race war. CHARLES MANSON'S GRANDDAUGHTER REVEALS MOMENT SHE DISCOVERED DARK FAMILY SECRET: 'IT WAS DEVASTATING' But after studying the previously unreleased recordings, Berlinger argues the murders were instead a desperate attempt to cover up "a series of blunders." "This whole idea of starting a race war was a false idea," Berlinger told Fox News Digital. "He certainly believed a race war was coming, or at least that's what he told his followers to control them. But the murders, in particular the Tate and LaBianca murders, were an attempt to get associate Bobby Beausoleil out of prison. He told his followers, 'He's my friend. You guys owe me a favor. Let's get him out of prison.'" "The truth is I believe, and others believe, that if they had succeeded in this crazy idea of getting Bobby Beausoleil out of prison, I think Manson would’ve killed him because he was a liability," said Berlinger. "But listening to those tapes made the story come alive, not these crazy conspiracy theories and myths that turned Charles Manson into the most mythologized figure in the history of true crime." Berlinger traces the chain of events that led to the murders to a botched drug deal. According to the documentary, Manson invited members of the Straight Satans motorcycle club to Spahn Ranch to protect him from the Black Panthers, whom he feared, offering them access to his female followers in exchange. "[Follower] Tex Watson tried to steal money from a drug dealer named Bernard ‘Lotsapoppa’ Crowe, who wants his money back," Berlinger explained. "Manson goes out there and doesn't intend to kill him, but thinks he killed him, a Black Panther." FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X According to the documentary, Watson stole Crowe's money, prompting Crowe to threaten retaliation. Manson later shot Crowe and mistakenly believed he had killed him. Crowe was not a Black Panther. "He goes back to Spahn Ranch and becomes paranoid that the Black Panthers are going to come after him. He becomes friends with Bobby, tells him to join the family and also to help protect the ranch. Bobby becomes tight with some bikers who were also invited to protect the ranch from the Black Panthers." But the motorcycle gang wanted more than just women. The documentary says Beausoleil brought them drugs he obtained from music teacher Gary Hinman. The bikers were unhappy with the quality of the supply, and Beausoleil was pressured to recover their money. "Bobby tries to get his money back from Gary and can’t get it," said Berlinger. According to court records, during the confrontation, Manson arrived at Hinman's home and slashed Hinman's face with a sword, cutting him from his left ear toward his chin. Over the course of about three days, Manson's followers tortured Hinman. Beausoleil later stabbed Hinman to death and wrote the words "Political Piggy" on a wall in Hinman's blood, along with an animal paw print intended to implicate the Black Panthers. "Gary Hinman is killed because Manson comes in, wields a sword and then tells Bobby 'finish the job' to cover the tracks," Berlinger said. SIGN UP TO GET THE TRUE CRIME NEWSLETTER Beausoleil was arrested about a week after Hinman’s body was discovered. Berlinger said Beausoleil was driving Hinman’s vehicle and had "the murder weapon stupidly in the stolen car." Berlinger said Manson wanted police to believe Hinman’s murder was the work of the Black Panthers to cast suspicion away from Beausoleil. He noted the attempt to free Beausoleil became the catalyst for the murders that followed. On Aug. 9, 1969, Manson's followers murdered five people at a Los Angeles home previously rented by music producer Terry Melcher: actress Sharon Tate, who was 8 1/2 months pregnant; coffee heiress Abigail Folger; celebrity hairstylist Jay Sebring; Polish writer Wojciech Frykowski; and Steven Parent, who had been visiting the estate's caretaker. Melcher had previously declined to sign Manson to a recording contract. "The murder is tried to be made to look like it was part of Gary Hinman’s murder," said Berlinger. "But when Manson picks up the paper the next day, and there’s no information about these two murders being linked, they do another murder. The logic is, ‘We’ve got to make people think that Bobby, who is sitting in prison, is not guilty.’" "This was all a series of blunders, a bunch of bad, spontaneous decision-making." GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB The next night, wealthy grocer Leno LaBianca and his wife, Rosemary LaBianca, were stabbed and killed in their home across town. The killers scrawled phrases including "Pigs" and the misspelled words "Healter Skelter" in blood at the crime scene. Manson was arrested in October 1969. Prosecutors maintained at trial that Manson ordered his followers to kill some of Los Angeles' rich and famous to trigger a race war, a plan prosecutors said grew in part from his interpretation of the Beatles' song "Helter Skelter." Manson frequently spoke about an impending race war and interpreted songs on the Beatles' "White Album" as messages about the coming conflict, according to testimony from his followers. What remains disputed is whether those beliefs motivated the Tate-LaBianca murders or whether, as Berlinger argues, prosecutors elevated them into the central theory of their case. "[Prosecutor Vincent Bugliosi] had to come up with a legal theory to convict a guy who actually didn’t do the killings," Berlinger said. "Manson wasn’t even there when the Tate-LaBianca killings took place. So how do you convict somebody who wasn’t there? Well, you come up with this organizing principle that he convinced his followers that a race war was coming, and he was trying to make that race war happen. It was a brilliant legal theory, but it’s a false story." "The Manson murders are much more tragic, but much more banal than this idea of some crazy cult trying to start a race war," Berlinger continued. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS "This was a drug deal gone bad, trying to cover up Gary Hinman’s killing by doing another murder the next day to make it look like a copycat murder, which were the Tate murders. And when that murder didn’t hit newspapers like a Black Panther murder, they did the LaBianca murders. It’s a series of blunders by people who were trying to cover their tracks, not this grand scheme of 'Helter Skelter.'" GOT A TIP? Bugliosi worked with writer Curt Gentry on a book about the case. Published in 1974, "Helter Skelter" became the bestselling true crime book of all time. Manson and three followers — Susan Atkins, Patricia Krenwinkel and Leslie Van Houten — were found guilty and later sentenced to death. Charles "Tex" Watson was tried separately and convicted later. Their death sentences were reduced to life in prison after the California Supreme Court invalidated the state's death penalty in 1972. Atkins died in prison in 2009. Van Houten was released on parole in 2023. Krenwinkel and Watson remain in prison. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE Manson died at a California hospital in 2017 while serving a life sentence. He was 83. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL Berlinger maintained Manson's reputation as an evil mastermind was fueled more by myth than reality. SEND US A TIP "He wasn’t killing or ordering people to kill to get some kind of satisfaction," Berlinger said. "He was covering up a series of blunders and just getting deeper and deeper into a hole. The best way to honor the victims is to be truthful about what happened."

articles.title: Witkoff and Kushner arrive in Moscow with plan to end war ahead of visit to Kyiv
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrive in Moscow, Russian state media report, ahead of a planned trip to Kyiv.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on Saturday, Russian state media reported, where they are expected to explore prospects for ending the war, now in its fifth year. Kirill Dmitriev, special representative of Russian President Vladimir Putin, was at Vnukovo airport to meet them, according to state media. After visiting the Russian capital Witkoff and Kushner are due to travel to the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, for the first time. However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Saturday that two airports near Kyiv had been struck by Russian missiles, including the airport at Boryspil, which used to handle international flights. “Evidently, these Russian strikes on airports are a reaction to discussions and preparations regarding the possibility of the American side using an aircraft to arrive in Ukraine,” Zelensky said. Since the war began, foreign leaders have traveled to Kyiv by rail from Poland. It’s unclear whether the reported Russian strikes will alter the US delegation’s plans. The US mission comes amid near-constant Russian missile strikes on the Ukrainian capital, including a direct hit on the Kyiv headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service, the SBU, on Friday. Zelensky has said that an acute shortage of air defense interceptors has left Ukraine vulnerable to ballistic missile attacks. Trump described Witkoff and Kushner as “great negotiators” at the White House on Friday, remarking that their dispatch is an effort to “see whether or not we can get something done.” But Russian officials have indicated that Moscow is not in the mood to compromise. “The US administration must take into account the realities on the ground in the matter of Ukrainian settlement, where the situation is changing not in Kyiv’s favor,” Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov told Russian state media TASS. Ryabkov suggested that Ukraine was struggling on the battlefield, and that the United States must consider this. A belt of important industrial towns in the eastern Donetsk region is under growing threat from Russian forces, which have inched forward in recent months. Zelensky has welcomed the prospect of Witkoff and Kushner’s visit, planned for Sunday. “Our goal is to have a visit and negotiations with the American side that are as constructive and substantive as possible. We need to look for realistic options on how to bring this war to an end,” Zelensky said on Friday. CNN’s Ivana Kottasová, Victoria Butenko, Jennifer Hansler, Kosta Gak and Darya Tarasova contributed reporting.

articles.title: At least 5 killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine as US envoys visit Moscow
articles.summary: Ukrainian armed forces were ordered to follow a three-day ceasefire as US envoys visit Moscow, before trip to Kyiv.
articles.body:
Russia has attacked the city of Kamianske in southeastern Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk region, killing five people and injuring five others, according to Governor Oleksandr Hanzha.

The attack came on Saturday morning, hours after several Ukrainian armed forces were reportedly ordered to follow a three-day ceasefire as United States special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner travel to Kyiv on Sunday and Moscow on Saturday with a proposal to “end the war”.

A separate local ceasefire was reportedly brokered ⁠by ⁠the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to enable ⁠repairs for the restoration of external power ⁠to the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, the agency said on Saturday.

The Russian-controlled nuclear power plant, ‌located in Ukraine, has been without external power since August 20 and has relied on emergency diesel generators to cool its vital safety systems.

Ukrainian media outlet Ukrainska Pravda reported that this “break” for Ukrainian forces was scheduled to start at midnight on September 5 and last until 23:59 on September 8.

“The military confirms that a ceasefire order has been received. The ceasefire is happening everywhere. On the ground, in the air, and at sea,” People’s Deputy Oleksiy Honcharenko wrote on his Telegram channel on Friday night.

However, this order did not stop Russian attacks from continuing in Ukraine overnight, according to the Interfax Ukraine news agency. As a result, Ukraine’s Armed Forces clarified that they did not have to order this temporary ceasefire on the front lines, as Russia had not stopped its aggression.

“The Russians struck a civilian enterprise in Kamianske, in the Dnipro region,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday on X.

“There were also demonstrative Russian strikes on our airports overnight – in Kyiv and Boryspil… Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport,” Zelenskyy added. “We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace.”

Apart from Kamianske, there were also reports of injuries from overnight Russian attacks in other parts of Ukraine. In the Odesa region, three people were injured, including a 17-year-old boy, the press service of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine reported on Facebook. In Mykolaiv, southern Ukraine, a 17-year-old girl was injured in an attack by Russian drones on a shopping centre.

In the Kyiv region, two women were injured and hospitalised, according to the head of Kyiv’s regional military administration, Tymur Tkachenko, after a Russian strike on a nine-storey residential building in Boryspil.

Civilian deaths in Ukraine have sharply increased over the past few months as Russia is using jet-powered drones, which fly at about half the speed of a passenger jet and are more difficult to intercept than propeller-powered drones.

Meanwhile, Russian military forces intercepted and destroyed 53 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight, including several over the Moscow region, the Russian Ministry of Defence announced on Saturday.

Over recent months, Ukraine has developed long-range drones that have repeatedly targeted Russia’s oil sector, hoping to dent the economy and the warehouses of online retailers to make the Russian public feel the effects of war.

On Friday, Trump told reporters that a peace deal in the more than four-year conflict has remained elusive due to what he described as a “personality problem” between the warring sides.

“President Zelenskyy and President Putin truly hate each other,” Trump said. “They have serious hate, and it’s getting in the way.”

According to Russian state news agency TASS, Witkoff and Kushner will be in Moscow on Saturday and Sunday, their first visit since January.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the duo would be in Ukraine on Sunday, marking their first visit to the country since Trump returned to power.

articles.title: Three cities, 16 years and $1 billion later, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art opens
articles.summary: Inside, lives a significant slice of Lucas’ private collection, spanning art, costumes, movie props and memorabilia, with more than 1,300 objects currently displayed across 30 galleries.
articles.body: In the gardens of the long-awaited Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, a 19th-century cast of Antonin Mercié’s sculpture of David conquering Goliath neighbors a bronze statue of Princess Leia strangling Jabba the Hutt with a chain. Rosie the Riveter stands by, her gaze averted. A collection of odd bedfellows, perhaps. But this party of underdogs also offer a fitting welcome to a sprawling new institution that, at every turn, argues that all forms of art and mythology on display here — from comic book illustrations and “Star Wars” concept art to Impressionist masterpieces and reproductions of the Sistine Chapel — are worthy of equal consideration within the long arc of human history. More than 16 years after first proposing a cultural institution dedicated to visual storytelling, filmmaker George Lucas and his wife, businesswoman Mellody Hobson, will open their long-awaited museum in Los Angeles on September 22. The project made two false starts — plans to construct it in San Francisco and Chicago were both eventually abandoned — and has cost Lucas around $1 billion of his own money to build (the recently opened Obama Presidential Center, for context, cost $850 million). Inside, visitors will find a significant slice of Lucas’ private collection, amassed over five decades and spanning art, costumes, movie props and memorabilia, with more than 1,300 objects currently displayed across 30 galleries. “This has been a long haul,” Lucas told reporters at a private press opening Wednesday. “Part of the problem is I’m a contrarian. I don’t like to do things that people think can be done.” “This one almost broke my will,” he added, “but the great people that we’ve assembled to do this has been a big advantage. We still had to deal with bureaucracies and people who have contrary thinking, but we managed to make our way through all that.” Many fans will come for the “Star Wars” vehicles and sculptures of Yoda and Grogu, but the sci-fi mega-franchise only occupies about 7% of the museum. Lucas and Hobson are betting those visitors will stay for artworks by Frida Kahlo and Norman Rockwell, photographs by Gordon Parks, comics by Frank Miller and Cowboy Bebop anime, which will be screened in one of two theaters alongside early silent movies, Lucas’ own student films and productions by famed historical artists like Man Ray. Considering the canon In recent years, major art institutions like New York’s Museum of Modern Art and London’s Tate Britain have reconsidered the cultural canon by rehanging their permanent collections, exhibiting overlooked or marginalized artists alongside more widely celebrated names. The Lucas Museum appears to follow a similar philosophy, contending that the gravitas of an artwork is not just determined by its display in space but by what it’s in dialogue with. Lucas has even called his namesake museum “a temple to the peoples’ art,” elevating the work of illustrators and other underappreciated art forms. The collection is elevated in a literal sense, too. Housed inside a sinuous white design by MAD Architects and Stantec, the Lucas Museum looks like a spaceship hovering above South Los Angeles’ Exposition Park. Architect and MAD founder Ma Yansong said, however, that he took inspiration for the 300,000-square-foot building from the forms of clouds. “The building is actually less about shape, and more about the experience inside the space,” he explained at the press preview. “I wanted to make the central plaza very spiritual, everyone (who) goes there can imagine something very different.” This lofty ambition can be felt everywhere, from the futuristic tube-like elevators to the surprise late addition of a top-floor exhibition dedicated to original Banksy murals, which some staff had not even yet seen. The museum defines narrative art as any art that tells a story, and, moving through the space, one feels the enormity of the task of organizing and presenting such a broad vision. “Narrative art is important because it depicts the myths that anchor us, the stories that we believe in,” Hobson said in her opening remarks alongside Lucas. “They may not necessarily be true, but they unite us as families, as communities, as countries, as nations.” The long view Downstairs, the opening “History of Narrative Art” exhibit feels more like a trip through a natural history museum, as if non-human visitors were being introduced to the great artifacts of human creativity displayed in glass portals or digitally projected onto gallery walls. This is where you’ll find recreations of ancient cave paintings, the Sistine Chapel, the Capitoline Wolf with Romulus and Remus, and a portrait of Henry VIII, mixing in reproductions and alternative ways of presenting works that couldn’t be physically brought into the museum. An elevator ride to the fourth floor brings you to where most of the museum’s collection is housed. Visitors can weave from a collection of Rockwell paintings, including the famous Civil Rights-era work “The Problem We All Live With,” to a room featuring Luke Skywalker’s X-34 Landspeeder. Some rooms are dedicated to individual artists, such as Rockwell and the fantasy artist Frank Frazetta. Others are organized by theme: adventure, romance, civic life. The open-plan, curvilinear design means the galleries are not fully divided, reinforcing the all-encompassing nature of the collection, though altogether the vast array of exhibits sometimes struggle for cohesiveness. Disjointed curation may reflect turbulence in the museum’s management ahead of the opening. Last April, former director and CEO Sandra Jackson-Dumont departed, with Lucas himself assuming responsibility for “content direction.” A month later, the museum laid off 15 full-time and seven part-time staff before chief curator Pilar Tompkins Rivas resigned in December, with no replacement planned. At the press preview, current CEO Tracey Bates maintained that Lucas has “always had a front seat with the curatorial.” She added: “He was always the lead curator. So that hasn’t actually changed. His vision’s always been the same.” Ever since the museum was first announced in 2010, critics have questioned whether it is a vanity project for the filmmaker (the $25 adult ticket prices and high membership fees have further irked his detractors). After failing to secure a site in San Francisco, Lucas faced public opposition and a lawsuit in Chicago, with nonprofit Friends of the Parks arguing that his lakefront proposal would essentially privatize public land. Amid the delays and setbacks, simply opening the museum may feel like a victory to its founders. For now, it’s unclear how they might handle future exhibitions, whether they’ll stage new displays from the permanent collection or look to commissions and loans. “We’re still figuring things out,” said senior curator and head of film, Ryan Linkof, at Wednesday’s press event, adding: “And we have all kinds of ideas for what comes next. “There are certain exhibitions that do need to be rotated, just by virtue of the fact that they’re works on paper — comics, photography, children’s book illustration, things that were made on fragile materials. There might be exhibitions that stay on longer. But there will always be something new to see at the Lucas Museum.”
